answers.answer: An HTTP cache stores response bodies and metadata for reuse; the browser private cache serves its user agent, while a CDN supplies shared edge caches near users. Origin is responsible for the resource. A hit finds a suitable reusable response; a miss lacks one usable for the request. Empty caches send GET browser → CDN → origin, returning origin → CDN → browser with storage only where policy allows. A browser hit needs no network request; another browser's miss can hit the CDN and avoid origin. Stored objects are HTTP responses, not database replicas; origin may consult a database, but hits need not. CDN request hit ratio is hits divided by requests reaching that layer: 800/1000 = 80%. Under the stated assumptions origin receives 1000−800 = 200 requests. Browser hits never reach this denominator, differing response sizes prevent interpreting it as byte savings, and real validation, background requests, extra layers and application/database work require separate measurements. Repeated public assets can reduce latency with nearby responses and reduce origin load and transfer. CDN request/transfer charges and key, invalidation and monitoring work must be weighed against measured reuse, latency and total cost. Omit shared caching for low-traffic mostly private or rarely reused Notes workloads when benefits do not justify costs; never weaken privacy for hit rate.

evidence.quote: An HTTP cache stores response bodies and metadata, such as status and headers, for reuse. A browser private cache serves that user agent. A content delivery network (CDN) runs shared caches at edge servers near users. The origin is the server responsible for the resource.

A hit reuses a suitable stored response; a miss lacks one usable for the request. With empty caches, the request goes browser → CDN → origin. The response returns origin → CDN → browser, with storage at each cache only if its policy permits.

A browser hit avoids the network request. After a browser miss, a CDN hit avoids origin. HTTP caches hold responses, not replicated database records. Origin may consult a database, but a hit need not reach it.
Request hit ratio is cache hits divided by requests at a specified layer.

Browser hits never entered that denominator. Request hit ratio is not byte hit ratio: response sizes differ. Revalidation, background refreshes, extra layers and application work need separate measurements in real traffic; 80% does not prove 80% less database work or transfer.

Repeated public assets and popular published pages can reduce latency by answering nearby, and reduce origin requests and transfer. CDN requests and transfer can incur charges; key configuration, invalidation and monitoring add operational work.
For a low-traffic application serving mostly private or rarely reused responses, omit shared caching if measured benefits do not justify those costs.

answers.answer: Cache-Control carries response caching directives. public explicitly permits shared caching subject to other rules; max-age sets freshness lifetime in seconds, and s-maxage overrides it only in shared caches. Fresh means young enough for reuse without validation under policy; stale means the lifetime has expired, without necessarily deleting the body. Age estimates seconds since origin generation or successful validation, including time through caches. With Age 90, browser lifetime 60 is exceeded by 30 seconds (zero freshness remaining); CDN lifetime 300 has 210 seconds remaining and is fresh. Delivery does not reset this clock; freshness is reuse permission, not evidence origin is unchanged. A representation is a returned form of a resource; revalidation checks continued usability. ETag is an opaque representation validator, preserved without interpretation. For stale v1 the CDN sends conditional GET to origin with If-None-Match: "v1", requesting a body only if the selected representation no longer matches. Unchanged origin returns 304 without a replacement body; CDN updates applicable metadata including freshness and serves its retained v1 body to the ordinary browser GET. Changed origin returns 200 with new body and ETag "v2"; CDN serves the new body and replaces stored representation if allowed. The validator does not push changes elsewhere. Validation saves body transfer on the validation hop for 304 but still contacts origin, which may run application/database work.

evidence.quote: Cache-Control is a response header carrying caching rules called directives. A fresh response is young enough for reuse without validation under its policy. A stale response has reached its freshness limit; its body need not be deleted. Freshness is permission to reuse, not proof that origin content is unchanged.
public explicitly permits shared caching subject to other rules. max-age sets the freshness lifetime in seconds. s-maxage overrides it only in shared caches; the browser still uses 60 seconds.
Age estimates seconds since generation or successful validation at origin, including time spent through caches.
Receiving it does not start a new full lifetime.

A representation is the returned form of a resource, such as a page's HTML. Revalidation checks whether the stored representation remains usable. ETag is an opaque validator identifying that representation; clients preserve the tag rather than interpreting it.
It sends a conditional GET to origin with If-None-Match: "v1", asking for the body only if the selected representation no longer matches.

If unchanged, origin returns 304 Not Modified without a replacement body. The CDN updates applicable stored metadata, including freshness information, and uses its retained body to answer the browser's ordinary GET.

If changed, origin returns 200 with the new body and its validator, for example ETag: "v2". The CDN replaces its stored representation if policy allows. An ETag does not push changes into other caches.
304 saves retransmitting the body across the validation hop. Origin was still contacted and may run application logic or query a database to decide whether the representation changed.

answers.answer: Cookies are browser-held state: Set-Cookie requests storage and Cookie sends it back. Authorization carries request credentials; authentication establishes identity whereas authorization checks resource permission. Use unqualified no-cache for the public page: storage allowed, successful validation required before every reuse. Use private for a note whose browser storage is acceptable: shared storage forbidden, browser storage allowed subject to other directives, without inherently requiring validation every use. Use no-store for the sensitive note: HTTP caches must not store it. This cannot erase delivered copies or substitute for permission checks. Cookies and Set-Cookie neither automatically create per-user entries nor universally prevent caching. Authorization requests have special shared-cache restrictions but response policy can permit reuse, so authentication is no universal bypass. A shared response given to a different user can expose private notes. Keep authorization at origin; verify explicit private/no-store response policies and actual CDN rules prevent shared storage and reuse, test different users, and do not label personalized content public.

evidence.quote: Cookies are browser-held state: Set-Cookie asks the browser to store it; Cookie sends it back. Authorization is a request header carrying credentials. Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks permission to access a resource.

For a public page, unqualified no-cache allows storage but requires successful validation before every reuse. It does not mean never store. For a private response where browser storage is acceptable, private forbids shared-cache storage; it neither forbids browser storage nor requires validation on every use. Other directives still apply.
For a sensitive response, no-store instructs HTTP caches not to store the response. It cannot erase previously delivered copies or replace permission checks.

A shared response reused for the wrong user can leak private data. Cookie and Set-Cookie do not automatically create per-user cache entries or universally prevent caching. Authorization-bearing requests have special shared-cache restrictions, but response policy can permit reuse; authentication alone is no universal CDN bypass guarantee.

Keep authorization at origin. For private routes, verify that explicit private/no-store policies and actual CDN rules prevent shared storage and reuse. Test different users; do not mark personalized responses public for a higher hit rate.

answers.answer: A cache key identifies the stored response that can satisfy a request, using method and target URL plus selected request headers. Variants are different returned forms of one resource. Preserve format=pdf versus format=html in matching and separate en versus fr. Vary names request headers whose values must match for reuse; Vary: Accept-Language separates language variants when honored. If the CDN ignores query parameters, verify its actual key settings retain format distinctions and language matching; correct the matching or bypass caching until both survive. Dropping format could serve HTML for a PDF request, and dropping language could return the wrong language. Keeping proven irrelevant tracking values fragments entries and reduces hits; remove only values confirmed not to change the response. Vary does not change URL, grant permission, or override private/no-store, so it cannot authorize sharing private notes.

evidence.quote: A cache key identifies which stored response can satisfy a request. HTTP caching uses the method and target URL, with selected request headers distinguishing variants: different returned forms of the same resource.

Keep the format query values distinct. A CDN configured to ignore them could return HTML for a PDF request; verify the actual key settings rather than assuming every CDN includes every query parameter.

Vary: Accept-Language tells a cache that this request header's value must match for reuse. It separates language variants when supported and honored. CDN support and custom keys differ: verify that both format and language survive the actual matching rules, or bypass caching until they do.

Irrelevant tracking parameters can create extra entries and fewer hits. Exclude them only after confirming they do not change the response. Vary does not change the URL, grant permission or override private/no-store. Correctly separated public variants are not permission to share private responses.

answers.answer: A versioned asset URL changes when its bytes change. Publish app.v2.js with changed bytes rather than overwriting app.v1.js, keep bytes immutable at each URL, and update the referring page to request v2. Long caching fits these immutable assets, but an old cached referring page can still request v1. For a mutable page retaining its URL, choose freshness/revalidation to match tolerated update delay, such as short freshness or validation on every reuse. A database edit does not rewrite stored responses. A CDN purge removes or invalidates targeted CDN entries according to provider behavior; verify relevant URL, variant and CDN-layer coverage, propagation and completion. It is not necessarily simultaneous everywhere and does not evict fresh browser copies or erase downloads. Unpublishing can stop future origin access and trigger purges but cannot instantly revoke delivered public content; choose lifetimes with this limit in mind.

evidence.quote: A versioned asset URL changes when its bytes change: publish app.v2.js instead of overwriting app.v1.js. Long caching fits immutable assets, whose bytes stay unchanged at each URL. Update the referring page to request v2; an old cached page can still ask for v1.

A mutable page that keeps its URL needs a chosen freshness/revalidation policy matching the tolerated update delay. A database edit does not rewrite stored HTTP responses. Short freshness or validation on each reuse makes a different trade-off from long-lived versioned assets.

A CDN purge removes or invalidates targeted CDN entries according to the provider. Verify coverage of the relevant URLs, variants and CDN cache layers, plus propagation and completion behavior. Purge is an operation to check, not an assumption of simultaneous replacement everywhere.

Purging CDN entries does not evict fresh browser copies or erase downloaded content. Unpublishing can stop future origin access and trigger purges, but already delivered public content cannot be instantly revoked. Choose cache lifetimes with that limit in mind before publishing.

answers.answer: stale-while-revalidate permits bounded stale serving while attempting background validation, hiding that latency. stale-if-error permits bounded stale fallback on eligible errors. They grant optional reuse permissions, not freshness or guaranteed availability. Freshness lasts 60 seconds and extensions count from its expiry. At age 75 the copy is 15 seconds stale, within the 30-second background-validation allowance ending at age 90, so it can be served while refreshed. At age 150 it is 90 seconds stale; an eligible origin error permits fallback within the 120-second error allowance ending at age 180. At age 200 it is 140 seconds stale, beyond both windows; neither directive authorizes stale reuse even with the same error. A cold cache has no fallback and expired allowances can expose failures. Support and policy must be verified; these permissions do not override private/no-store, and private-data correctness or urgent removal may prohibit stale reuse despite its public-help availability benefit.

evidence.quote: When a public response tolerates delay, stale-while-revalidate permits bounded stale reuse while attempting background validation, hiding validation latency. stale-if-error permits bounded stale fallback on eligible errors, such as an origin failure. These are optional permissions, not freshness or availability promises.
The response is fresh for 60 seconds; stale windows start when freshness expires.

At age 75 it is 15 seconds stale: the additional 30-second background-validation window permits reuse while refreshing, through age 90. At age 150 with an eligible error, it is 90 seconds stale: the error allowance lasts another 120 seconds after expiry, through age 180. At age 200 neither extension still permits stale reuse.

A cold cache has no response to fall back to, and exhausted allowances can expose the failure. Verify provider support and policy; these directives do not override private/no-store. Private-data correctness or urgent removal may forbid stale reuse even when it improves public-help availability.
